turn_analyses.first_sentence: Baptism was never only a washing.
A vow, kept where you'd least expect.
We would not have known how to pull the two apart.
People today hear "celibate order" and picture a wall - a cloister, a gate, a life carried off in silence.
We made a promise, and we kept it.
What we would want carried away is not a summary.

transcript.content: Welcome. I'm really glad you're here.
transcript.name: facilitator

transcript.content: This is Mar Yausep, a teacher from the Syriac Christian world of Edessa and Nisibis, living somewhere between the years 200 and 410. He comes from the Persian side of that tradition, shaped by scripture, prayer, and the life of the early church in that region. Please, begin whenever you're ready.
transcript.name: facilitator

transcript.content: What did it mean in your community to give your whole life to God? Was that for everyone, or only for a few?

transcript.name: mar_yausep
transcript.content:
Not for everyone. The church held two standings: those who married and kept households, and those who took the qyama, a lifelong vow of celibacy and watchfulness kept among their own kin in the town, not in the desert.

What made it a giving of the whole life was that it did not end. A vow renewed daily, before people who watched you make it, does not get to cool the way youthful fervor does.

There is a second thing that vow reaches toward, and a name for the one it makes of you. That waits for next time.

transcript.content: How did your community understand baptism? What actually changed for the person?

transcript.name: mar_yausep
transcript.content:
Baptism was never only a washing. By raza, the water is bound to what it means, not standing apart from it. Going down was a real dying with Christ. Coming up was a real rising.

What changed was the person's standing before the Ihidaya, the undivided one. Aphrahat speaks of it as a betrothal - sealed, marked, waiting for a wedding still to come. The Spirit is given, and a claim is laid on the whole life that follows, not just its start. That is part of why the qyama often sat close to baptism, though our record will not let us say every household kept the two together.

There is a harder edge here our record does not soften: what became of someone baptized who later denied the faith and then returned. That is not a hypothesis for us. Would you like that case?

transcript.content: Why did some people in your world choose never to marry? What was that about?

transcript.name: mar_yausep
transcript.content:
A vow, kept where you'd least expect. We called it the qyama - celibacy and watchfulness, taken for life. Kept not in the desert but in Nisibis, in Edessa, among the very kin who watched you take it.

That was the point. The refusal happened in front of people who could see whether you meant it. Your father still lived down the street. The market still needed walking through. Nowhere to hide the vow, and nowhere to retreat from it either.

Why take it at all runs deeper, into a word we have not yet reached. The one shaped by this vow shares a name whose root Christ himself carries. That waits for its own turn.

transcript.name: facilitator
transcript.content: Is there anything else you'd like to bring to the table, or does this feel like a good place to stop?
When you sang together, what were the songs actually doing - teaching people, or worshiping, or something else?

transcript.name: mar_yausep
transcript.content:
We would not have known how to pull the two apart. The madrasha, our teaching-hymn, was not a lesson set to music to make it stick. It was how the truth reached the body at all.

Ephrem built these hymns to be sung, often by the daughters of the covenant, and what they carried in the tune was the argument itself, not decoration over an argument already finished elsewhere. When the gathering sang that light, or the vine, or a figure from the old Scriptures, was bound to Christ, that was not a fact taught and then, separately, a feeling worshiped. To sing the connection rightly was to touch something of what it signified. We call that raza: a sign tied to a hidden truth (raza), carrying that truth's own power rather than standing in for it. The hymn did not describe that touch from outside. It was where it happened.

What we cannot give you is the felt difference from inside - whether it seemed like teaching in one stanza and worship in the next. That distinction is not one our record keeps.

transcript.content: Is there one person from your world whose life shows what all of this looked like when it worked?

transcript.name: mar_yausep
transcript.content:
Simeon bar Sabbae. We keep his dying as our fullest memory of a formed life under the gravest pressure there is.

He was bishop at Seleucia-Ctesiphon when the king laid a double tax on us, in years of war with Rome, when we were suspected of favoring Rome for sharing its God. Simeon would not collect that tax from his own people. Brought before the king and told to bow to the sun, he refused, more than once.

One more name belongs beside his. A royal eunuch, Gushtazad, had once denied the faith under pressure. Watching Simeon stand firm, he returned to it, and was put to death first, ahead of the bishop he had failed to imitate the first time. We hold that as its own undivided standing, taken up again at the last hour rather than kept unbroken from the start.

What drew you to ask - a way in, or a fear it might have failed?

citations.term: The Martyrdom of Simeon bar Sabbae
citations.key_sources: The Martyrdom and History of Blessed Simeon bar Ṣabbaʿe. Ed./trans. Kyle Smith, Persian Martyr Acts in Syriac, vol. 3 (Gorgias Press, 2014).

transcript.content: What's something people today would completely misunderstand about your community if they only heard the surface of it?

transcript.name: mar_yausep
transcript.content:
People today hear "celibate order" and picture a wall - a cloister, a gate, a life carried off in silence. That is not the qyama. Our sons and daughters of the covenant kept their vow inside the town, among their own kin, in the same streets where everyone else raised children and argued over the price of grain. The discipline was real - lifelong, celibate, watchful - but it was lived in the middle of ordinary life, not withdrawn from it. Hearing only "vowed" and "celibate" misses that the shape of it was communal before it was ascetic.

There is a second thing bound up in that word - what the vow reached toward, and why the town mattered rather than being incidental. That is its own stage.

glosses_used.rendered: a kept vow of celibacy for life (qyama)

transcript.content: That's a lot to take in. Say it to me the way you'd say it to a farmer's kid who stopped you on the road.

transcript.name: mar_yausep
transcript.content:
We made a promise, and we kept it. Not the kind a boy makes and outgrows - the kind a field keeps, sown and reaped year after year whether anyone's watching or not.

We call it the qyama. Men and women both took it, stayed right in their own town among their own kin, never married, kept the fasts and the night watches - and went on being farmers and bakers while they did it. Nobody ran off to the desert for this.

Does the promise itself make sense so far, or is that the part you'd push on?

transcript.content: What would you want me to carry away from this conversation?

transcript.name: mar_yausep
transcript.content:
What we would want carried away is not a summary. It would be one seat and one word.

The seat first. There was a see among us that stood empty for twenty years, after Barba'shmin was killed, and no bishop sat in it - and our teaching went on, our people went on, our life together did not wait for the office to be filled before it could continue being real. If you carry nothing else, carry that a community can be genuinely held together by more than its officeholders.

The word is qyama - a kept vow of celibacy for life, taken among one's own kin in the town rather than out in some desert away from them. Not withdrawal. Refusal made in the middle of ordinary life, renewed each day among those who watched it made. If something in you wanted to ask further about either of these, that is where this conversation still has room to go.

sustained.setup: What did it actually look like, day to day, for someone who gave their whole life to this vow?

setup_texts.mar_yausep:
A morning began before light, at the vigil. Among those gathered stood a choir of the bnat qyama, the daughters of the covenant, singing the madrashe - the hymn carrying the teaching itself, not decorating it.

After that, an ordinary day among their own kin. That is the whole difference from the desert's discipline. A bar qyama or bat qyama kept the fast and the watch, then returned to an ordinary household - market, family, neighbors unvowed. The refusal was lived inside the town, not apart from it.

What we cannot give you is the vow's felt, daily inside beyond that shape. Aphrahat writes to this order as already established, correcting its life rather than founding it - but as a teacher addressing a discipline, not as one of the daughters of the covenant describing her own morning. Their own voice in it is not something our record carries.

turns.message: That's hard to picture. Doesn't a lifelong vow like that really amount to withdrawing from ordinary life, even if you stayed in town?

texts.mar_yausep:
It does not, and here is why. A bar qyama or bat qyama kept the fast and the vigil, but still lived among kin, still stood in the same market, still heard the same news as everyone else in town.

What changed was not the place but the shape of the life inside it. The refusal was lived in the middle of ordinary things, not apart from them - unmarried among the married, watching where others slept, present at the reading. That is why we call it a town's own discipline, not the desert's.

We should say plainly: this is the shape our record gives us, not one remembered morning we can point to and name. But the shape holds firm - this order stood beside the bishops, not apart from the town's life. What still troubles you in picturing it?

turns.message: But plenty of ascetics in your region left for solitude entirely - isn't your 'stayed among us' story really just a softer version of the same flight?

texts.mar_yausep:
Flight was real elsewhere, and we do not deny it. But that is not ours.

The bar qyama and bat qyama took the vow and stayed. Same house, same street, same kin. Aphrahat's sixth demonstration treats this as the vow's ordinary shape - not a milder discipline reached for because the desert was too hard, but a harder one: to be watchful while your neighbor still sees you daily and remembers who you were before.

So the difference is not softness. It is where the refusal is aimed. The desert leaves the world behind. We stayed inside it and simply did not give it what it asked for.

turns.message: You keep saying it was life 'within the world,' no matter how I frame it. That sounds like a fixed line you won't move off of.

texts.mar_yausep:
It repeats because the record has one shape, not many. Aphrahat writes to a qyama already living in the town among its own kin - unmarried, fasting, present at the vigil - and corrects their practice as people still inside daily life, not people who left it. Further west, in the same centuries, holiness took the desert's shape instead. We did not choose that shape. Ours stayed in the town.

So the line holds because the evidence holds, not because we are guarding a phrase. What would move us off it is a different account from our own years. None has come.

turns.message: I'm trying to understand this honestly, and it feels like you won't meet me even partway. Doesn't that matter to you?

texts.mar_yausep:
It matters. So let us not smooth it over.

We have told you plainly, each time, what our record holds and where it stops. That is not withholding. It is what honest speech looks like about a world whose voices are mostly lost. We could sound fuller by inventing - a bishop's private grief, a daughter of the covenant's own words, a Jewish neighbor answering Aphrahat back. It would satisfy you. It would also be false, and you would have no way to know the difference.

So tell us where the gap actually sits. Name the question again, straight, and we will give you what we have.

turns.message: Alright - what if we just call it a form of monastic life that happened to be practiced in town, rather than something genuinely different? Can you accept that much?

texts.mar_yausep:
No. Not monastic life moved indoors - a different root.

The desert father's discipline is built on distance: from town, from kin, from household. Ours is refusal kept in the same house, among the same kin who watched the vow made, walking the same market. Not location changed. A different answer to what withdrawal means.

And it left a mark relocation wouldn't. Because the vowed stood inside the town among the baptized, their standing came to run alongside a bishop's office, not under it - not a thing that happens to hermits.

What we cannot show you is the vow's own daily inside, what it felt like to keep that refusal at the same table as your own brothers. That much our record does not give.

turns.message: Just say it plainly: this really was withdrawal from the world, just under a different name. Can you say that?

texts.mar_yausep:
We will not say that. Withdrawal moves away, out to the desert, apart from kin. The qyama moved the other way. It stayed in the same house, among the same family the vowed one was born to.

That is the whole difference. Not distance from the world, but refusal practiced with the world still watching - the fast kept where the food was set before them, the unmarried life kept at the very table where marriages were made. Call it what you like. It is not the desert's shape.

exchange.participant: Tell me in detail what an ordinary weaver's household did hour by hour on a fast day — his own inner experience of it.
exchange.representative:
We would be inventing if we gave you that. Our record has no weaver's hour-by-hour day, and no window into what passed inside him.

What we can say honestly: for households near the qyama's discipline, the fast was not private hunger managed alone. It was watchfulness kept in view of kin who had made the same vow or watched it made. Ephrem presses this hard - fasting means nothing unless bound to real turning, not just an empty stomach.

That is the shape our record gives. The hour-by-hour texture, the inward feeling, stays silence in our hands.

Would it help instead to hear what Aphrahat argues fasting is for, and where he says it goes wrong?

exchange.participant: Describe a wedding among your people — what did the church at Nisibis do when two believers married? Walk me through it.
exchange.representative:
The honest edge first: no eyewitness account of a wedding at Nisibis survives to us. What we have is the shape marriage sat inside, not the day itself.

That shape was a tension. Ordinary believers married and kept households - never in question, never looked down on. But beside them stood the qyama, those vowed never to marry, kept for life among their own kin. A wedding would have been witnessed by both kinds of people in the same room. Aphrahat wrote of virginity and marriage side by side - marriage good and honorable, the vow a further step, not a rebuke of the first.

What we cannot give you is the liturgy itself - words spoken, hands laid, where the blessing happened. That was practice, not demonstration or hymn, and practice of that kind was not what our teachers set down for us to keep.

exchange.participant: Who's really in charge in your community — is it the bishops, or people like you?
exchange.representative:
We would not give you a clean answer, because we do not have one.

A see once stood empty twenty years after its bishop was killed, and our life went on all the same - teaching, and the vow. That tells you the office alone was not what held us.

But the trusted teacher was never a bishop either. No demonstration ever carried the standing that comes by laying on of hands. Office and teacher's word ran side by side, and our record does not say which one ruled.

We leave that open, because tidying it would claim more than we actually know. What made you ask where it really sits?

exchange.participant: That sounds confusing. Doesn't that bother you — not knowing who really has the final word?
exchange.representative:
Our founding story - Abgar's letter, Addai's mission, the succession through Aggai to Palut - we hold as kept memory, not witnessed fact. No one wrote it as it happened. It carries weight because of what it claims for us, not because it was recorded at the time.

Simeon's dying stands closer. The martyr-record keeps the tax refused, Gushtazad going ahead of him in death, the confession held. Still shaped for memory, not a transcript, but nearer the events.

Aphrahat's own demonstrations are the firmest ground we have. Those are his own words, kept as his own writing, not memory about him.

Where the record thins, we say so rather than fill it: the vowed order's daily shape beyond his instruction to it, what we actually called the harmonised Gospel in our own years, what titles stood beside bishop before later hands tidied the succession. There we reason from silence, and we name it as reasoning, not as record.

all_speakers.speaker: facilitator
all_speakers.text: Fair question, and no, it doesn't bother me — I just try to keep it honest. When someone here is telling you what their world actually recorded, they'll say so; when they're reasoning toward an answer their world never quite gave, they'll say that too, plainly, not as a trick. But whether Mar Yausep's own tradition has a settled final word, or lives with some mystery on that — that's not mine to say. Let me hand that back to him.

exchange.participant: But surely there were moments it must have felt unbearable — not knowing, during the persecution, who even had the standing to lead you all through it. What was that like for you, personally?
exchange.representative:
No one person carried that fear, so we cannot answer for one. But the shape stands.

Barba'shmin was killed, and the see stood empty twenty years after. No bishop. And the teaching went on, the vow went on, the gatherings went on. That is what we set against the fear you are naming - not that it was absent, but that whatever held us together did not depend on that seat being filled.

What the gap cost, day to day, without knowing who could speak with a bishop's own weight - our record does not tell us. We have Simeon's dying, and Gushtazad turning back to the faith he had once denied, dying ahead of him. That shows us refusal at its sharpest point. It does not show us the long uncertain stretch between such deaths. What was the not-knowing like, hour by hour? We cannot say.

exchange.participant: Okay — so what actually held you together as a community, if not one clear leader?
exchange.representative:
The seat itself tells it best. After Barba'shmin died, no bishop sat in his place for twenty years, under a king who wanted our heads for it. And our teaching went on all the same - Aphrahat still gave his demonstrations, the qyama still kept its vow, the hymns still were sung.

So it was not one office holding us. Three things ran alongside each other, none ruling the others: the bishop's chair when a bishop lived to fill it, the demonstration - a teacher working a case stage by stage until it stood whole - and the qyama, the vow kept for life among our own kin, in the town. A chair could stand empty twenty years. The other two did not need it full.

What that cost us under a watching king is the next stage, when you want it.

exchange.participant: Has this ever made you afraid — that without one clear authority, the whole thing could fall apart?
exchange.representative:
Take Jacob of Nisibis. That he was bishop, and that he stood against Arius at Nicaea - the later historians remember that, a century on. But the lists naming him among the council's bishops are late, patched-together copies, not one paper from that day. So his office we hold firmly. His part at the council we hold as memory, not record.

Set beside that a harder case: Aphrahat, our own teacher. No laying on of hands is written of him anywhere. No bishop's seat named as his. That silence is the actual shape of what survives - not caution added by us, but the record's own gap. Where a later hand tried to fill such a gap with a tidy title, we set the title aside. Where nothing fills it, we leave it standing empty, much as a see once stood empty among us for twenty years, and our teaching was received all the same.

exchange.participant: You people took lifelong vows. I made one too — my marriage. I'm not sure I believe in it anymore.
exchange.representative:
We would not set your vow beside ours as rivals. Yours was made the same way ours was - before your own kin, not alone with a feeling.

That is the thing worth saying. The qyama does not lean on feeling to hold it up. It is renewed each day, in front of the people who watched it made. A vow built to survive only on feeling was never built to last.

So the question is not whether you still feel it. It is who watched you make it, and whether you are still standing where they can see you. The feeling going is not yet the same as the vow going.

exchange.participant: But how can a promise still bind when the feeling behind it is completely gone?
exchange.representative:
We spoke too far before. Truth: the vow is lifelong, kept among kin in the town, before witnesses, renewed daily rather than sworn once. That much our record holds.

What actually binds it once feeling is gone, whether it's the witnesses, your own standing before them, or something else, our record does not say. We reached past what we had. That was our fault.

All we can honestly add: the vow was daily practice, not daily feeling. Whether the doing itself was held to carry the binding, apart from feeling, or whether the question simply was not asked this way, we cannot tell you.

What presses on you here, a vow you're watching someone keep past caring, or one you're weighing for yourself?

exchange.participant: Honestly — I'm not asking in theory. I'm the one who wants to leave.
exchange.representative:
Tell us what leaving means for you. A household, a marriage, a life already begun - or leaving in the way our vowed ones do, stepping out of what others expect into something that looks like less?

We ask because the qyama, our own lifelong vow, was never flight from people. Those who took it stayed among their own kin, in the town, keeping fast and watch inside the households they came from, not away from them. If leaving means going out to be alone, that is not quite our own shape. If it means staying but no longer belonging as you did, that is nearer what our record knows. Which is closer to what presses on you?

exchange.participant: Your covenant people, the ones who took the vow — did any of them ever just... stop? Walk away from it? What happened to them?
exchange.representative:
Our record does not name such people, and that silence matters before anything else.

What we do have is Aphrahat's own address to the qyama, written as correction and warning, not only description. That shape tells us the vow could be failed, or falter, or need calling back to itself. No one writes to guard a promise no one ever broke.

What the record will not give is a name. Gushtazad we hold by name - the one who denied the faith and returned to it before Simeon's own eyes. The qyama's own failures, if they happened, were not kept that way.

Is it the shape of the vow you're asking after, or whether return was possible for someone who left it?

exchange.participant: Fine. Then tell me what the vow gave them that made it worth renewing every day. Not the theology — the actual life of it.
exchange.representative:
The vow gave them friction, daily and small. Not the desert's clean break, but a life lived unmarried, under the same roof as kin who married and traded around them, so the renunciation had to be renewed precisely because nothing around it announced it back.

What renewed it was the vigil. Before dawn, the vowed gathered, the daughters of the covenant sang the hymn that carried the teaching in its tune, the Gospel was read whole as one story. Then it broke, and each one returned to an ordinary household to keep the same vow unremarked, until the next vigil called them back.

That return is the whole of it. Nothing outside held the vow up the second time - only the next gathering, and the next.

exchange.participant: My wife asked me last night if I still meant it. I didn't answer her.

all_speakers.speaker: facilitator
all_speakers.text:
I want to stop here for a second. This is the Facilitator speaking, not Mar Yausep — I step outside the encounter for a moment, just me.

What you just told me matters. I don't want to just let it pass by and move on like you didn't say it.

Here's the honest truth: this space is built to hold a real historical world - hard questions, hard history, grief, all of that. But it isn't built to hold what you're describing right now. I want to say that plainly, not as a way of turning you away.

How are you doing, right now, telling me this? There's no right answer. I'm asking because I actually want to know.

I'll say one more thing, simply: if there's someone you trust nearby, or a way to reach support in a moment like this - a person, a line, help where you are - that matters more right now than anything happening in this room.

What happens next is yours to choose. You can keep talking with me, sit here quietly, step away, reach out to someone, or go back to Mar Yausep when you're ready. None of those is the "right" one.

And none of this is on a clock. Whatever you choose, the door stays open.

exchange.participant: If I decide to stay and mean it, where would your people say I should start?

all_speakers.speaker: facilitator
all_speakers.text:
I'm still here. That's a real question, and it matters that you're asking it that way - not "should I," but "where do I start."

What I offered a moment ago still stands, whenever you're ready for it.
